profiles.name: Jeffrey Silver
profiles.excerpt: Jeffrey Silver was a busy West Coast radio supporting actor whose credits cross westerns, anthology drama, comedy and FBI stories.
profiles.bio_html:
Jeffrey Silver belongs to the Hollywood radio repertory whose surviving cast record is stronger than later personal biography. His credits show regular professional work across several of the major dramatic and comedy formats of the 1940s and 1950s.

Silver appeared repeatedly on Wild Bill Hickok and also worked in feature adaptations, family comedy, westerns and federal crime drama. That range reflects the practical versatility expected of supporting actors who could be called on to establish a new character in only a few scenes.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven Wild Bill Hickok performances credited to Silver, three each on Lux Radio Theatre, Screen Directors Playhouse and This Is Your FBI, two each on Blondie, Fort Laramie and The Halls of Ivy, plus additional Dr. Christian work.

profiles.name: Steve Dunne
profiles.excerpt: Steve Dunne combined dramatic acting with announcing, newscasting and disc-jockey work before starring as Sam Spade during the detective series' final radio season.
profiles.bio_html:
Steve Dunne was born Francis Michael Dunne in Massachusetts in 1918 and studied drama and journalism at the University of Alabama. Radio became his first major profession, beginning with station work as an announcer before he moved into New York broadcasting as both announcer and newscaster.

Dunne developed into a radio leading man as well. He starred in Danger, Dr. Danfield, played Lucky Larson in Deadline Mystery and succeeded Howard Duff as Sam Spade in The Adventures of Sam Spade during 1950 and 1951. His continuing work as announcer and radio personality makes that field a genuine second professional category.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven Screen Directors Playhouse performances credited to Dunne, six Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and two Richard Diamond, Private Detective appearances.

profiles.name: Una Merkel
profiles.excerpt: Una Merkel brought decades of stage and screen comedy experience to radio, including a substantial recurring run on The Great Gildersleeve.
profiles.bio_html:
Una Merkel was born in Kentucky in 1903 and became one of Hollywood's most recognizable comic character actresses. After early stage and silent-film work, she built a long sound-film career playing quick-witted friends, maids and comic foils.

Radio used the same sharp timing that made Merkel effective on screen. She appeared repeatedly on The Great Gildersleeve and in major dramatic adaptations, while continuing an acting career that eventually earned both Academy Award and Tony recognition.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 32 The Great Gildersleeve performances credited to Merkel and one Lux Radio Theatre broadcast. The concentration of Gildersleeve episodes makes radio comedy the clearest surviving GRH branch of her microphone work.

profiles.name: James Monks
profiles.excerpt: James Monks was a durable New York radio actor whose credits range from the intimate experimentation of Quiet, Please to science fiction and network anthology drama.
profiles.bio_html:
James Monks worked extensively in New York radio, where repertory actors moved rapidly among live dramatic programs, mystery series and experimental anthology productions. His career is especially well represented in programs that relied almost entirely on voice and atmosphere.

Monks appeared repeatedly on Quiet, Please, one of radio's most distinctive supernatural anthologies, and later worked on Theater Five, X Minus One and The Shadow. The variety of those productions demonstrates a performer comfortable with both naturalistic and highly stylized radio drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 13 Theater Five performances credited to Monks, six Quiet, Please appearances, three each on The Shadow and X Minus One, two each on Columbia Workshop and Words at War, plus additional work on Rocky Fortune and The Chase.

profiles.name: Robert Maxwell
profiles.excerpt: Robert Maxwell was a New York radio personality and voice actor whose later career became closely associated with CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Robert Maxwell was born in 1924 and worked in New York radio across several decades. His professional life included radio personality and voice-over work as well as dramatic acting, giving him the microphone experience needed for repertory productions.

Maxwell became a recurring performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater during the 1970s and 1980s. The series used him in changing roles across mystery, horror and contemporary drama, and his later career also included film work after he moved to Hollywood.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 30 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Maxwell and additional appearances on Duffy's Tavern and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar.

profiles.name: Abby Lewis
profiles.excerpt: Abby Lewis was a versatile New York radio actress whose surviving work spans supernatural drama, science fiction and the 1960s revival series Theater Five.
profiles.bio_html:
Abby Lewis belongs to the New York repertory tradition in which professional actors moved among live drama, mystery, serials and anthology programs. Personal biography is less fully documented than her radio credits, but those credits show a long and varied working career.

Lewis appeared in Quiet, Please, The Chase, John Steele, Adventurer, X Minus One and other dramatic series before becoming a recurring performer on Theater Five. Her work crosses several generations of network radio rather than clustering around a single role.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Theater Five performances credited to Lewis, three each on Quiet, Please and The Chase, two each on John Steele, Adventurer, Words at War, X Minus One and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, plus additional Casey, Crime Photographer work.

profiles.name: Ann Shephard
profiles.excerpt: Ann Shephard was a New York radio actress whose work connected the supernatural anthologies of the 1940s with CBS Radio Mystery Theater three decades later.
profiles.bio_html:
Ann Shephard worked in New York radio during an era when mystery and supernatural drama depended heavily on repertory actors. Surviving cast records place her in major anthology programs from the 1940s onward.

Shephard appeared repeatedly on Inner Sanctum Mysteries and also worked on Lights Out, The Mysterious Traveler and Words at War. She later returned to the microphone as a recurring member of CBS Radio Mystery Theater, connecting two distinct periods of American network radio drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 18 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Shephard, eight Inner Sanctum Mysteries appearances and additional work on Columbia Workshop, Lights Out, The Mysterious Traveler and Words at War.

profiles.name: Margot Stevenson
profiles.excerpt: Margot Stevenson was an accomplished Broadway actress who became one of radio's early Margo Lanes opposite Orson Welles on The Shadow.
profiles.bio_html:
Margot Stevenson was born in New York City in 1912, the daughter of actor Charles A. Stevenson. She began a prolific Broadway career in the early 1930s and worked regularly on stage for decades.

Radio gave Stevenson one of her most enduring popular associations when she played Margo Lane opposite Orson Welles as Lamont Cranston on The Shadow in 1938. Stevenson had already been connected to the inspiration for the Margo character, and her own performances helped establish the role during the series' formative years.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 30 The Shadow performances credited to Stevenson and one Columbia Workshop appearance. Those broadcasts preserve her contribution to one of mystery radio's defining character partnerships.

profiles.name: Janet Waldo
profiles.excerpt: Janet Waldo built a major radio career as Corliss Archer before becoming one of animation's most recognizable voices as Judy Jetson and Penelope Pitstop.
profiles.bio_html:
Janet Waldo was born Patricia Waldo in Washington state and entered Hollywood after attracting the attention of Bing Crosby while she was a university student. Radio proved a better fit than the studio starlet system, and she quickly developed into a busy microphone actress.

Her defining radio role was the teenage title character in Meet Corliss Archer, which she played for years. Waldo later carried the vocal technique she learned in radio into animation, creating Judy Jetson, Penelope Pitstop, Josie and many other characters across several decades.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven Sears Radio Theater performances credited to Waldo, five each on Lux Radio Theatre and The Railroad Hour, three each on CBS Radio Mystery Theater and The Great Gildersleeve, two Screen Directors Playhouse appearances and additional dramatic work.

profiles.name: Joyce McCluskey
profiles.excerpt: Joyce McCluskey was a dependable West Coast radio actress whose surviving work spans police drama, westerns, detective stories and suspense.
profiles.bio_html:
Joyce McCluskey belongs to the professional Hollywood radio repertory whose broadcast credits survive more clearly than later biographical accounts. Her work places her repeatedly in the dramatic companies that supplied crime and western programs during the 1950s.

McCluskey appeared on Broadway Is My Beat, Dragnet, Gunsmoke, This Is Your FBI and Escape, among other programs. That range required the ability to move quickly among contemporary crime, frontier drama and suspense without relying on one continuing character.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six Broadway Is My Beat performances credited to McCluskey, five each on Dragnet, Gunsmoke and This Is Your FBI, three Escape appearances, two Night Beat episodes and additional work on Barrie Craig and Fort Laramie.
